As at 2026-11-06, the installation of an amusement ride in Singapore is governed by the Amusement Rides Safety Act 2011, and the statutory text reproduced in your sources is the consolidated version in force from 18 December 2023; Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for any later amendment [CITE:1] [CITE:4]. The sources do not reproduce the definition of "amusement ride" and do not use the term "fairground ride", so whether, and how, this Act applies to your ride cannot be confirmed from them [CITE:1] [CITE:2].

## 1. A valid installation permit is the starting point

A person must not install, or cause any amusement ride to be installed, unless the installation is authorised by a valid installation permit and is carried out in accordance with that permit's conditions [CITE:2]. Installing without such authorisation, or causing or authorising installation works that contravene this requirement, is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $200,000 or imprisonment not exceeding 2 years or both, plus a continuing-contravention fine of up to $1,000 per day and, if the contravention continues after conviction, a further offence carrying up to $2,000 per day [CITE:2]. The Commissioner may also require the cessation of non-compliant installation works by written notice and may take the necessary steps at the person's expense and recover the reasonable costs through a civil suit [CITE:2].

## 2. The substantive conditions the installation must satisfy

Section 7(2) places a duty on the permit holder, on every person directly engaged in carrying out the authorised installation works, and on the qualified person supervising them, to ensure that the installation works are at all times carried out in accordance with four things [CITE:7]:

- the design and specifications and the proposed installation method and programme, as authorised by the installation permit [CITE:7];
- the conditions of the installation permit [CITE:7];
- the prescribed requirements (the requirements specified in the subsidiary legislation, which your sources do not reproduce) [CITE:7]; and
- any direction given by the Commissioner in respect of the installation works [CITE:7].

In addition, no installation works may be carried out except under the supervision of a qualified person, and a permit holder who breaches that requirement commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $100,000, with the imprisonment term cut off in the excerpt provided [CITE:7]. A person directly engaged in the installation works who deviates, or permits or authorises a deviation, in any material way from the authorised design and specifications or proposed installation method and programme commits an offence unless that deviation has been submitted to and approved by the Commissioner under the regulations, punishable by up to $100,000 or 12 months' imprisonment or both [CITE:10].

## 3. What must be in place before the permit is issued

The Commissioner may issue the permit in such form or manner as the Commissioner determines, subject to such conditions as the Commissioner thinks fit to impose; alternatively, the Commissioner may direct the applicant, at the applicant's own expense and within a specified time, to make required alterations or amendments to the design and specifications and the proposed installation method and programme, and to take specified measures so that the installation works conform to the prescribed requirements, with the source excerpt ending at that point [CITE:1]. If a direction of that kind is not complied with within the stated time (or any further period allowed), the Commissioner may dismiss the application [CITE:4].

The Commissioner must not issue an installation permit unless satisfied that [CITE:4]:

- the applicant is a fit and appropriate person and satisfies the prescribed requirements [CITE:4];
- the design and specifications and proposed installation method and programme have been reviewed under section 46 by a qualified person and certified by that person as conforming to the prescribed requirements [CITE:4];
- where applicable, the plans for any building works forming part of, or connected to, the ride have been approved or deemed approved by the Commissioner of Building Control under sections 5, 5A or 5AA of the Building Control Act 1989 [CITE:4];
- the design and plans of the ride's fire and rescue management system have been approved by the Commissioner of Civil Defence under section 36(3)(a) [CITE:4]; and
- the installation works will be supervised by a qualified person appointed by the applicant, who may be the same or a different person from the design reviewer [CITE:4].

Before applying, the applicant must appoint a qualified person (or separate qualified persons) to review and certify the design, specifications and proposed installation method and programme; to supervise the installation works; and to inspect and certify the ride under section 12 on completion [CITE:1]. The applicant must also apply to the Commissioner of Civil Defence for approval of the design and plans of the ride's fire and rescue management system [CITE:1].

## 4. Qualified persons: independence and standard of care

A person must not appoint a qualified person who has, or ought reasonably to be known to have, a professional or financial interest in the ride, its operation, or the relevant installation works, and a qualified person with such an interest must not act [CITE:18]. A qualified person must exercise the standard of skill, care and diligence reasonably expected of a specialist professional engineer with the requisite specialised knowledge and experience for functions of a similar nature, scope and complexity [CITE:17]. For a major amusement ride, the qualified person must appoint and consider the advice of a conformity assessor unless the Commissioner grants a waiver, and a non-compliant certificate may then be refused [CITE:17].

If the appointed qualified person vacates the appointment at any of the three key stages, the holder and the qualified person must each notify the Commissioner within 14 days, a substitute must be appointed within the time allowed and notified within 7 days, and the consequences differ by stage [CITE:6] [CITE:9] [CITE:12]:

- Before the permit is issued, the Commissioner must not consider the application until the substitute has been appointed, notified, and has reviewed and certified the design, specifications and installation method and programme [CITE:6].
- During installation works, the installation works must be ceased until the substitute is appointed and notified, and breach of that requirement is an offence carrying up to $100,000 or 12 months' imprisonment or both, plus continuing daily penalties [CITE:9].
- Before the section 12 inspection or certification is carried out or completed, a substitute must be appointed and notified within the stated periods [CITE:12].

## 5. Certification after installation

On completion, the qualified person appointed for the inspection must inspect the ride and issue a certificate stating that the installation works were properly carried out in accordance with the authorised design, specifications and installation method and programme, the permit conditions, the prescribed requirements, and any Commissioner direction, and that the ride as installed conforms to the prescribed requirements and is in a safe working condition and fit for operation [CITE:3]. The permit holder must also obtain from the Commissioner of Civil Defence a certificate of compliance for the ride's fire and rescue management system [CITE:3].

## 6. Compliance duties and enforcement during installation

The permit holder, any person directly engaged in the installation works, and the supervising qualified person must notify the Commissioner, as soon as practicable, of any contravention of the Act relating to the carrying out of the installation works that they know or ought reasonably to know of [CITE:14]. Breach of that duty is an offence carrying up to $20,000 or 3 months' imprisonment or both, with a defence available to a person who proves they did not know and could not reasonably have discovered the contravention [CITE:14]. The Commissioner may direct that installation works cease, require remedial measures at the expense of the person directed, and withhold written consent to resumption until the requirements are met [CITE:7]; failing to comply with such a direction, or resuming without the written consent, is an offence carrying up to $100,000 or 12 months' imprisonment or both [CITE:10]. An installation permit may also be revoked on grounds including a contravention of its conditions or of a Commissioner direction, fraud or misrepresentation, or the public interest, and may be suspended for a specified period, with a hearing normally required before revocation or suspension [CITE:8]. The permit also lapses automatically if the supervising qualified person vacates the appointment and the holder fails to appoint and notify a substitute [CITE:8]. Where a ride is installed in a manner or condition posing an imminent danger, the Commissioner may direct that installation or operation cease, that the ride be closed or cordoned off, and that specified measures be taken to secure, stabilise or dismantle it, with failure to comply carrying criminal and civil-cost consequences [CITE:11].

## 7. Conditions can be changed; the permit cannot be transferred

The Commissioner may alter the conditions of an installation permit at any time, either on the Commissioner's own volition or on the holder's application [CITE:5]. On the Commissioner's own initiative, written notice must be given stating the proposed alteration and allowing at least 14 days for written representations, which the Commissioner must consider before issuing a written direction specifying the alteration and the date from which the altered conditions apply [CITE:5]. A holder's application must be made in the form the Commissioner requires, specify the alteration and the reasons for it, and be accompanied by the required documents and the prescribed fee [CITE:5]. An installation permit is not transferable, and any purported transfer is void [CITE:15]. The issue of a permit does not confer, or prove, any title to or interest in the land on which the ride is or is to be installed [CITE:16].

## 8. Appeals

A person aggrieved by the Commissioner's refusal to issue an installation permit, alteration of permit conditions on the Commissioner's own volition, revocation or suspension of a permit, or the giving of notices or directions affecting installation works may appeal to the Minister in the prescribed form and within the prescribed time [CITE:13]. The Minister may dismiss or allow the appeal unconditionally or subject to conditions after hearing the appellant's written representations, and the Minister's decision is final [CITE:13]. An appeal does not itself suspend the revocation, suspension, notice or direction, which takes effect from the date specified by the Commissioner unless the Minister otherwise directs [CITE:13].

## 9. Gaps in the sources provided

The sources do not reproduce the Act's definitions of "amusement ride", "qualified person", "major amusement ride" or "prescribed requirements", nor the regulations prescribing the fee, forms, and technical requirements [CITE:1] [CITE:4]. For those points, the Act's definitions and the subsidiary legislation on Singapore Statutes Online are the relevant places to look [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, based on the supplied consolidated provisions, your fairground ride’s installation must be supervised by a **qualified person** appointed by the installation-permit holder. The Commissioner must not issue the installation permit unless satisfied that the installation works will be carried out under that person’s supervision. [CITE:3] [CITE:8]

The permit holder must ensure that no installation works are carried out except under the qualified person’s supervision. [CITE:1]

The permit holder, every person directly engaged in the installation works, and the supervising qualified person must ensure that the works comply at all times with the authorised design and specifications, installation method and programme, permit conditions, prescribed requirements, and any direction from the Commissioner. [CITE:1]

A person seeking an installation permit must appoint qualified persons to review and certify the design, supervise installation, and inspect and certify the ride after installation; the same qualified person may perform all three functions, or different qualified persons may be appointed. [CITE:8]

If the supervising qualified person leaves while installation is underway, both that person and the permit holder must notify the Commissioner within 14 days. The holder must appoint a substitute within the time allowed by the Commissioner, notify the Commissioner of the substitute appointment within seven days thereafter, and cease the installation works until those steps are completed. [CITE:2] Failure to appoint and notify a substitute can also cause the installation permit to lapse automatically. [CITE:4]

As at 2026-11-06, the power to order a post-mortem examination of a dead animal or bird comes principally from the Animals and Birds Act 1965.

**Animals and Birds Act 1965**

- The **Director-General or an authorised officer** may cause the carcase of any animal or bird to be subject to a post-mortem examination. [CITE:1]
- They may do so through written directions, which may require a carcase that has already been buried to be exhumed for the examination, and require the carcase to be delivered to an authorised examiner at a specified place and time. [CITE:1]
- An **authorised examiner** may also conduct a post-mortem examination on the carcase of an animal or bird examined under section 19, that is, where the Director-General or an authorised officer has reason to believe the animal or bird may be infected with disease. In that process the examiner may destroy the animal or bird and examine its carcase, if that is the appropriate method in accordance with accepted veterinary practice for determining whether the animal or bird has a particular disease. [CITE:2]
- A person who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with a written direction under section 22, or without permission removes a carcase from the place to which it was delivered, commits an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months, or both. [CITE:1]

**Animals at licensed slaughter-houses**

- The **Director-General** may, in writing, direct the owner or occupier of a licensed slaughter-house to subject the animals intended for slaughter there to a post-mortem examination after slaughter, carried out by an authorised examiner. [CITE:10]

**Related but distinct powers, and the position for human bodies**

- An authorised officer or a police officer may give written directions requiring the destruction of an incurably diseased or severely injured animal, with the expenses of removing and burying the carcase borne by the owner; that is a power to order destruction rather than to order a post-mortem examination. [CITE:18]
- Where an animal is reasonably suspected to have died of disease, its carcase must not be moved without the written permission of the authorised officer, and it may be buried if no instructions are received within 24 hours of the report of the death. [CITE:11]
- The separate regimes for human bodies do not extend to animals or birds: a Coroner may order a post-mortem examination of a human body after consulting a pathologist, and must do so if directed to do so by the Public Prosecutor. [CITE:4] The Director-General of Health may order a post-mortem examination of the body of a person who died while being, or suspected of being, a case or an at-risk individual of an infectious disease. [CITE:6]

As at 2026-11-06, **yes, provided the animal-health officer is an “authorised officer” under the Animals and Birds Act 1965**. Section 26 permits an authorised officer to direct the disinfection or destruction of specified articles—including bedding, harness, fittings, buckets, pails and utensils—that were used in connection with an infected animal or bird. [CITE:1]

The directions **must be written**, because section 26 expressly empowers the officer to “give written directions” for either disinfection or destruction. [CITE:1]

A person who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with such written directions commits an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment not exceeding six months, or both. No compensation is payable for articles destroyed under section 26. [CITE:1]

The supplied wording uses the term “authorised officer” but does not state which offices or job titles qualify, so it does not establish that every person called an animal-health officer automatically has this power. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, land-survey records do not have to be kept on paper: the Boundaries and Survey Maps Act 1998 expressly permits the Chief Surveyor to maintain survey records and plans in electronic media or by any other means. [CITE:1]

**Electronic maintenance by the Chief Surveyor**

- Section 6(1) of the Boundaries and Survey Maps Act 1998 makes it the Chief Surveyor's duty to assign lot, strata lot and accessory lot numbers, to maintain all survey records, to make copies of survey records and plans available on payment of prescribed fees, and to perform other functions specified in the Act or other written law. [CITE:1]
- Section 6(3) states that the survey records and plans for any land may be maintained by the Chief Surveyor "in any electronic media or other means", so the statute imposes no paper requirement. [CITE:1]
- The statutory office is the "Chief Surveyor", defined as the person appointed under section 3 of the Boundaries and Survey Maps Act 1998. [CITE:13]

**How plans and documents enter the records**

- On completion of a cadastral survey, the registered surveyor who signs the plan must deposit the plan, field books, calculation sheets and survey data with the Authority "in any form that the Authority may approve". [CITE:3]
- Once the plan is approved by the Chief Surveyor, the deposited plan and survey documents become property of the Authority and must be filed as permanent survey records. [CITE:3]
- A cadastral survey is not complete until the survey plan has been approved by, and filed in the office of, the Chief Surveyor. [CITE:8]
- No cadastral survey or survey plan may be accepted or adopted for the purpose of any written law unless approved by the Chief Surveyor, and an assurance plan lodged in the Registry of Deeds or the Land Titles Registry must be signed by a registered surveyor, approved by the Chief Surveyor, and bear a caution that the boundaries, dimensions and areas are inconclusive. [CITE:10]

**Evidential effect and public access**

- A certified copy of a deposited survey plan or survey document signed by the Chief Surveyor is received in evidence without proof of signature as prima facie proof of the matters contained in it. [CITE:3]
- A printout of information stored in a computer in the Authority, issued and signed by the Chief Surveyor, is also received in evidence as prima facie proof of the matters contained in the document. [CITE:3]
- A certified plan is prima facie evidence of the boundaries and boundary marks of the parcel, and of its area and lot number. [CITE:8]
- Copies of survey records and plans are available from the Chief Surveyor on payment of prescribed fees, and the Chief Surveyor may provide certified copies of deposited plans and documents on payment of the prescribed fee. [CITE:1] [CITE:3]

**Related electronic-record rules**

- Under the Planning Act 1998, the competent authority must keep a record of permissions granted or refused and of Ministerial appeal decisions, including all relevant plans, make that record available for inspection on payment of prescribed fees, and may keep the record in electronic form. [CITE:2]
- Where another rule of law requires a document, record or information to be retained, the Electronic Transactions Act 2010 allows satisfaction of that requirement by an electronic record if the information remains accessible and usable, is retained in its original format or a demonstrably accurate format, information identifying the origin, destination, date and time of sending or receipt is retained, and any additional supervising-agency requirements are met; the section does not apply where a rule of law expressly requires electronic retention or the Minister has excluded the matter by Gazette order. [CITE:5]
- Where a rule of law requires an original document or record, the Electronic Transactions Act 2010 permits an electronic record if there is reliable assurance of integrity from the time the document was first made in its final form, the electronic record is capable of being displayed to the person receiving it, and any additional agency requirements are complied with; integrity means the information has remained complete and unaltered apart from changes arising in the normal course of communication, storage and display. [CITE:16]
- The Land Titles Act 1993 defines "approved form" to include an electronic form produced by electronic copy, image or reproduction of a written instrument, and "electronic instrument" as an instrument in electronic form. [CITE:13]

**What these sources do not settle**

- The requirement in the Registration of Deeds Act 1988 for plans to be annexed to a caveat, and for the Government survey lot number maintained in the Chief Surveyor's records to be stated, is expressed without specifying any particular medium. [CITE:9]
- The actual prescribed fees referred to in the survey-record provisions are set outside the text of the section itself, and are not stated in the provided material. [CITE:1]

**As at 2026-11-06, the owner of the land is responsible for preserving its boundary markers.** The law works as follows.

**1. The basic duty to preserve**
Section 10(1) of the Boundaries and Survey Maps Act 1998 provides that every owner of land must preserve the boundary marks erected on the boundaries of the land [CITE:1]. A "boundary mark" includes any survey stone, iron pipe, spike, or other survey mark authorised by law for the purpose of marking boundaries [CITE:9].

**2. Repair or replacement, and who pays**
Where the Chief Surveyor becomes aware that a boundary mark or survey control mark has been injured, destroyed or removed, or needs repairs, the Chief Surveyor may cause the mark to be replaced or repaired and recover the costs as a debt due to the Singapore Land Authority (the Authority) from the owners of the lands for which the marks serve as boundaries, in any proportion the Chief Surveyor considers proper [CITE:1]. Where the marks serve as boundaries of two or more parcels, those owners must bear the replacement or repair costs (including the cost of a cadastral survey ordered by the Chief Surveyor) in the proportions the Chief Surveyor considers proper [CITE:1].

**3. Clearing boundary lines**
A survey officer may serve a notice on a person who owns or has an interest in land subject to a cadastral survey, calling on that person to clear any boundary line [CITE:7]. If the person fails to do the work, the survey officer may carry it out and recover the cost from that person as a debt due to the Authority [CITE:7].

**4. Criminal liability for damage**
Any person who wilfully obliterates, removes or injures, without reasonable excuse, a boundary mark or survey control mark that was made or erected by, or under the direction of, the Chief Surveyor commits an offence punishable on conviction by a fine of up to $1,000, and may further be required by a Magistrate’s Court to pay three times the cost of replacing and repairing the mark and of any survey made necessary by the offending act [CITE:6]. If an offender cannot be found, the Chief Surveyor may direct replacement or repair and order the cost to be paid by the owners of the adjacent lands in proportions the Chief Surveyor considers proper [CITE:6].

**5. Special rules in national parks and nature reserves**
Within any national park or nature reserve, a person must not knowingly destroy, damage, deface, alter or remove a boundary mark, and conviction carries a fine of up to $20,000 [CITE:4]. The same provision also prohibits wilfully or negligently destroying, damaging or defacing any object of zoological, botanical, geological, ethnological, scientific or aesthetic interest in such areas [CITE:4].

**6. Related duty where the land adjoins State land**
If your land abuts on State land, every owner or occupier must define and keep defined the boundary between that land and the adjoining State land by a wall, bank, drain, fence, road, path or other sufficient means showing the whole extent of the boundary, and the Collector may require you by written notice to define or renew the boundary [CITE:5].

**7. The public authority role**
The Singapore Land Authority is responsible for managing and maintaining the cadastral survey system in Singapore as a foundation for land title and for regulating the conduct of cadastral surveys [CITE:18], and the Chief Surveyor may, in the course of a cadastral survey, alter, repair or remove boundary marks and place new boundary marks on the land [CITE:8].

As at 2026-11-06, under the supplied consolidated text, you must lodge the adjudication application **in writing with an authorised nominating body**, addressed to that body. [CITE:3] The authorised nominating body then refers the application to a registered adjudicator it considers appropriate to determine it. [CITE:4]

Before lodging the application, you must have notified the respondent in writing, containing the prescribed particulars, of your intention to apply for adjudication. [CITE:3] The application must also be made within seven days after your entitlement to apply first arises. [CITE:3]

As at 2026-11-06, the “authorised nominating body” must open and maintain with a bank a **trust account** for holding the adjudicated amount paid to it under section 18(3). [CITE:1]

The account must be a current or deposit account in the body’s name and must bear the exact words **“BCISOPA ANB — Adjudicated Amount Client Account”** in the account title at the bank. [CITE:1]

The arrangement is subject to these rules:

- Interest earned on adjudicated amounts held in the trust account accrues to the authorised nominating body, which may dispose of it as it considers fit. [CITE:1]
- Money may be withdrawn only for that permitted disposal of interest or to make a payment under section 22(3). [CITE:1]
- Money in the trust account is ring-fenced: it is not available to pay the body’s debts and cannot be taken or paid under a court enforcement order or process. [CITE:1]
- This ring-fencing does not prejudice any lawful claim that a claimant or respondent has against money held in the trust account. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, yes. Section 7(1) of the Control of Plants Act 1993 prohibits a person from importing fresh fruit or vegetables for sale, supply or distribution except under, and in accordance with the conditions of, a licence issued by the Director-General. [CITE:2]

A separate permit is also required for each consignment imported. The importer must obtain a consignment permit from the Director-General and carry out the import in accordance with that permit’s conditions. [CITE:1]

For fresh vegetables, the consignment requirements include that the whole shipment conforms to the permit description; contains no prohibited pesticide residue and does not exceed prescribed pesticide or toxic-chemical residue levels; complies with prescribed sanitary standards; is supported by satisfactory compliance evidence; and has containers bearing the producer’s name, address and any other prescribed particulars. [CITE:1]

A licence application is made to the Director-General with the prescribed fee and any requested particulars, information or documents; the Director-General may issue the licence with or without conditions, or refuse it. [CITE:3]

Failure to import under a licence or contrary to its conditions can constitute an offence, punishable on conviction by a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. Failure to comply with the consignment-permit requirements carries the same maximum penalty. [CITE:2] [CITE:1]

Under the Food Safety and Security Act 2025, non-compliance with licence conditions may also support regulatory action against a licensed importer, including modification of the licence or suspension; an unlicensed-import offence under section 7(4) of the Control of Plants Act is classified as a “relevant offence” for this purpose. [CITE:9] [CITE:4]

## The certification process under the Food Safety and Security Act 2025

- Division 4 of Part 14 (general licensing procedures) applies to every application to be appointed a certified pesticide operator, subject to modifications for this particular division [CITE:6].

- The Agency's criteria for appointment are in section 211, and it must have regard to the prescribed qualifications and practical experience and to the applicant's suitability, the applicant's compliance history with appointment conditions, the Act and applicable codes of practice, whether regulatory action under section 213 has been or is being taken or contemplated, any available information about relevant convictions, and whether it is otherwise not in the public interest of Singapore for the applicant to be or continue to be certified [CITE:3]. The Agency is not confined to those listed matters and may take into account any other relevant matters and evidence [CITE:3].

- The Agency may, with the Minister's approval, make "pesticide control regulations" dealing with matters connected with appointment as certified pesticide operators and applications for appointment, training and qualification requirements, tests for applicants, record-keeping and returns, and standards and procedures for the use of plant pesticides [CITE:13].

- The provided extracts reproduce only the cross-reference to Division 4 of Part 14 and not that Division or the regulations themselves, so the precise application form, required particulars and filing method are not stated in these sources [CITE:6][CITE:13]. ## The previous route under the Control of Plants Act 1993

- Under section 12 of the Control of Plants Act 1993, a person desiring to be certified as a pesticide operator applied to the Director-General, who certified the applicant if satisfied of the prescribed qualifications and practical experience and that the applicant was fit and proper to be entrusted with the safe use of pesticides [CITE:1]. The Director-General referred to in that Act is the Director-General, Plant Health [CITE:20].

- The Second Schedule of the 2025 Act preserves proceedings for suspension or cancellation of pesticide operator certification that were started under section 13 of the Control of Plants Act 1993 and were pending immediately before the commencement of section 209, allowing them to continue under that Act [CITE:7].

- Section 331 of the 2025 Act amends section 2 of the Control of Plants Act 1993 by deleting the definition of "certified pesticide operator" from that Act [CITE:19].

## Why the certification matters

- Under section 11 of the Control of Plants Act 1993, a person must not use any pesticide in the cultivation of any plant unless the pesticide is registered and the person is a certified pesticide operator or the use is supervised by a certified pesticide operator, and the person must also ensure proper storage, proper container disposal and that residue on cultivated plants does not exceed the prescribed level [CITE:11].

- Under section 214 of the 2025 Act, an individual commits an offence if they carry on, cause or permit prescribed pesticide work for reward and are neither a certified pesticide operator authorised for that kind of work, nor working under the direction or supervision of such an operator, nor exempt under sections 320 or 321 [CITE:10]. The penalty on conviction is a fine not exceeding $15,000 or imprisonment not exceeding six months or both, rising for a repeat offender to a fine not exceeding $30,000 or imprisonment not exceeding twelve months or both [CITE:10].

**As at 2026-11-06**, the position under *The Subsidiary Management Corporation No. 01 – Strata Title Plan No. 4355 v Janaed & Anor* [2022] SGHC(A) 26 is as follows.

**MCST's argument.** MCST contended that it could reasonably rely on Zoe, its independent contractor, to provide a safe system of work, the requisite safety equipment and/or supervision; on that footing, MCST said it had not breached its duty of care [CITE:3]. This was argued in the context of MCST's engagement of Zoe to replace two flow switches at another chiller in the mechanical and electrical ("M&E") room of Westgate Tower, where Janaed later fell from a third chiller [CITE:1].

**The framework for the breach issue.** By that stage, the question was not whether a duty of care existed — the court had already held that MCST owed Janaed a duty of care, with the standard of care informed by MCST's duties under the Workplace Safety and Health Act ("WSHA"), the Workplace Safety and Health (Work at Heights) Regulations 2013 ("WH Regulations"), and the *Code of Practice for Working Safely at Heights* [CITE:10].

**Why the court rejected it.** The Appellate Division rejected the reliance argument outright [CITE:3]. Under Part IV of the WSHA, persons who create or have control over safety risks at workplaces "will not be allowed to shelter behind each other or others to avoid liability when those risks materialise" [CITE:3]. Because MCST was an "occupier" under the WSHA — a person with charge, management or control of the premises, whether or not also the owner — it had primary responsibility for safety in the M&E room and could not avoid liability by sheltering behind its contractor, Zoe [CITE:3] [CITE:17].

**MCST's related submissions.** MCST also argued that the cost of installing guard-rails or barriers was excessive or disproportionate, that they were impracticable, and that they were not part of industry practice; however, no evidence of industry practice was adduced in support, and the court noted that MCST could instead have provided a mobile elevated work platform, which is one of the fall prevention systems under the Code [CITE:3] [CITE:10]. The court accordingly agreed with the High Court Judge that MCST breached its duty of care [CITE:3].

As at 2026-11-06, MCST’s primary position was that it was not liable to Janaed in negligence. [CITE:7]

As at 2026-11-06, *[2018] SGCA 41* explains that *Spandeck* established a **single test for determining a duty of care in tort**, applicable to all negligence claims regardless of whether the loss is physical, pure economic or relational economic loss. [CITE:1] [CITE:4] [CITE:6]

A duty of care arises where:

1. **Factual foreseeability is satisfied**—it is factually foreseeable that the defendant’s negligence might harm the plaintiff. [CITE:8]  
2. **There is sufficient legal proximity between the parties**—the plaintiff must be so closely and directly affected by the defendant’s conduct that the defendant ought to have the plaintiff in contemplation. [CITE:8]  
3. **Policy considerations do not militate against imposing the duty**. [CITE:8]

Legal proximity includes **physical, circumstantial and causal proximity**, as well as the defendant’s voluntary assumption of responsibility and the plaintiff’s reliance on the defendant. [CITE:13] Relevant proximity factors include the defendant’s knowledge of the risk, reliance or plaintiff’s vulnerability, and the defendant’s control over the situation coupled with the plaintiff’s corresponding vulnerability. [CITE:13]

*Spandeck* rejected the general rule that pure economic loss was recoverable only if it followed physical damage to person or property. The precise classification of the loss is therefore immaterial when deciding whether a duty of care arises, and a plaintiff need not establish physical damage to property. [CITE:1] [CITE:6] [CITE:36]

The concern that such a rule might create liability to an indeterminate class is addressed through the proximity requirement, because sufficient proximity limits the class of persons to whom the defendant may owe a duty of care. [CITE:5] The test is applied incrementally with reference to decided cases. [CITE:3]

As at 2018-12-31, the Court of Appeal dismissed SRA’s appeal and held that SSA was not liable in negligence for the losses caused by the first flood on 24 December 2014. [CITE:13]

The Court departed from the High Court’s reasoning: instead of finding that SSA had breached its duty of care but that the breach had not caused the losses, the appellate court held that SSA had not breached any duty it owed to SRA and, independently, that SSA’s actions had not caused the losses. During the renovation period, control of the premises had passed to Sport SG, which engaged HCJ to carry out the drainage and embankment works. As SSA neither designed nor controlled those works and could not carry out alterations without Sport SG’s consent, the Court found no duty of care during that period and no causal proximity between SSA and the slope failure. [CITE:12] [CITE:17] [CITE:19]

After SSA regained control on 1 December 2014, it still owed SRA a duty to take reasonable care to eliminate dangers that SSA actually knew or ought reasonably to have known about. However, there was no evidence that SSA knew or reasonably ought to have known of the poor design or construction that caused the landslip. [CITE:18]

For purposes of the appeal, the Court did not uphold the High Court’s newly formulated duty that SSA make inquiries and conduct checks on the premises’ drainage capabilities, because that duty had not been raised in the parties’ pleaded cases. [CITE:14] [CITE:18]

As at 2026-11-06, under the reasoning in [2018] SGCA 42, an entrant must establish more than the existence of a duty of care: the entrant must prove both **breach of duty** and **causation of the claimed loss**. [CITE:4]

**Breach:** The entrant must show that the occupier failed to exercise reasonable care to eliminate a danger that the occupier actually knew, or ought reasonably to have known, about. An occupier is not an insurer of safety, and what constitutes reasonable care depends on the particular facts. [CITE:5] [CITE:9]

**Causation:** The entrant must prove on the balance of probabilities that the occupier’s breach caused the losses complained of. The test is whether the entrant would not have suffered those losses **“but for”** the occupier’s negligent acts or omissions. [CITE:4]

Accordingly, even if an entrant establishes a duty and identifies deficient conduct by the occupier, the entrant must still connect that breach to the claimed loss; liability does not follow merely from the existence of a duty or a failure of reasonable care. [CITE:4] [CITE:5]

As at 2026-11-06, **[2018] SGHC 272** states that *Animal Concerns* establishes that a company director is not immune from liability for the director’s **own tort** merely because the tort relates to the company’s affairs or because the company has a separate legal personality. [CITE:6] [CITE:9]

The relevant distinction is between liability for the **company’s acts** and liability for the **individual’s own tort**: where the alleged wrongdoing is committed personally by the director, the corporate-veil argument does not preclude liability, whereas merely suing someone for conduct committed as the company’s organ may engage the corporate-veil principle. [CITE:9]

If the director personally commits the tort, the director may be personally liable, and the company may also be vicariously liable where the tort was committed in the course of the director’s employment. [CITE:9]

The court also explained that *Animal Concerns* is consistent with the proposition that a director may be personally liable for either fraudulent or negligent representations; personal liability depends on the director’s own conduct and, for negligent misrepresentation, whether the director conveyed an assumption of personal responsibility. [CITE:5] [CITE:3]

Accordingly, *Animal Concerns* does **not** make every director personally liable for statements made on the company’s behalf. It establishes that corporate status alone is no bar to personal liability for the director’s own tort, while leaving the question of personal responsibility or an assumed duty to be determined on the facts. [CITE:4] [CITE:15]

As at 2026-11-06, in the discussion of *Su Ah Tee* in [2018] SGHC 272, the property purchasers claimed damages from the solicitors who had acted for them in the property purchase on **two grounds: breach of contract and negligence** [CITE:3].

As at 2026-11-06, the Court of Appeal explained that *Sisters of Charity* did not require proof that the tarred mops were the precise cause of the fire; the uncertainty did not prevent an inference of negligence under *res ipsa loquitur*. [CITE:3]

Thus, the decision did not conclusively establish that the mops started the fire. It treated the negligent storage of the mops at the place where the fire occurred as sufficient to support the *res ipsa loquitur* inference. [CITE:4]

As at 2026-11-06, the passages supplied from [2016] SGHC 118 cover the introduction to the appeal, the appellants' policy submissions, and the court's discussion of the "doctrine of ultra-hazardous acts"; they do not contain a separate passage recording the defendants in the Singapore case itself as contending that the plaintiffs could not recover payments as damages [CITE:1][CITE:2][CITE:5][CITE:11]. The only discussion of "payments" and damages within the supplied material is the Singapore judge's account of the facts and arguments in the English Court of Appeal decision in *Honeywill and Stein Limited v Larkin Brothers (London's Commercial Photographers) Limited*, which he recounted as the leading authority on the doctrine [CITE:5].

**The contention recounted in the judgment**

In that English case, the plaintiffs hired the defendants to photograph the interior of a cinema; the defendants' employee negligently set up a chemical flashlight too close to a curtain, the magnesium powder ignited the curtain and the resulting fire caused considerable damage [CITE:5]. The plaintiffs, acting on advice, paid the cinema's owners before suing the defendants for an indemnity [CITE:5]. The defendants' contention was that no damages were recoverable because the plaintiffs had no legal liability to pay up, the defendants being independent contractors; the claim was disallowed at first instance and reversed on appeal [CITE:5].

The argument therefore had two elements: first, the payment was not a legally recognised loss because the plaintiffs were not under a legal obligation to make it — they had paid on advice; and second, the defendants' status as independent contractors meant they could not be answerable for the resulting damage [CITE:5].

**Why the Singapore judge treated that authority as an exception, not the general rule**

The judge explained that the cases such as *Honeywill* establish the "doctrine of ultra-hazardous acts": there are certain acts which are so dangerous that a person who procures their performance cannot escape liability if harm is caused by their negligent performance, even if the act was performed by an independent contractor [CITE:5]. This sits alongside the general rule that an employer is not liable for the acts of an independent contractor, and the competing principle that "a person causing something to be done, the doing of which casts on him a duty, cannot escape from the responsibility attaching on him of seeing that duty performed by delegating it to a contractor" — the language of non-delegable duties [CITE:11].

**The outcome in [2016] SGHC 118 itself**

The appeal concerned demolition works performed by Esthetix Design Pte Ltd on the respondents' property, debris having fallen on the appellants' property and caused damage [CITE:2]. The District Judge's findings that Esthetix was an independent contractor, that the respondents had exercised reasonable care in selecting it, and that the works were not "ultra-hazardous" were upheld: the respondents were not vicariously liable and bore no personal liability, because they had neither failed to exercise due care in selecting the contractor nor owed the appellants a non-delegable duty arising out of the demolition works [CITE:2]. The appellants' argument that the policy considerations of effective compensation for victims, loss-spreading and deterrence of future harm, or a "close connection" between the risks posed by the works and the harm suffered, justified imposing vicarious liability was not accepted [CITE:1].

If the specific contention made by the defendants in the Singapore case about recovery of payments is what you need, it falls outside the paragraphs supplied; the full published judgment (available through the Singapore Courts' judgment repository) and, if necessary, a lawyer's assistance would be the places to check [CITE:2].

As at 2026-11-06, the second issue in [2016] SGHC 118 was whether the respondents were personally liable for **failing to exercise reasonable care in the appointment (selection) of their independent contractor, Esthetix** — a form of liability the court called "negligent selection liability". [CITE:3]

That liability is **personal and primary**, meaning the legal responsibility flows from the employer's own failure to exercise reasonable care in the selection process, rather than from the contractor's negligent acts; it can therefore arise even where the employer is not vicariously liable for the contractor's torts. [CITE:3]

The applicable standard of care is that of a reasonable person in the circumstances of the defendant, and a complete tort of negligence requires causation, so a failure to make checks would only matter if it would have revealed that the contractor was unsuitable or given a reason not to appoint it. [CITE:4]

As at 2026-11-06, the principal live liability issue was whether the fire was caused by the defendant’s negligence. Initially, the defendant admitted that the fire started in Unit 141 and spread to Unit 143; the disputed questions were the fire’s cause and whether the defendant was negligent. [CITE:3]

The broader issues were: (1) whether the fire began in Unit 141 or Unit 143; (2) if it began in Unit 141, whether the defendant caused it negligently; and (3) if it began in Unit 143, whether the plaintiff caused it negligently. As at 2026-11-06, the answer is as follows.

**Amount claimed.** In *Union Concept Manufacturers Pte Ltd and another v Rhythme Technology Pte Ltd* [2015] SGHC 121, the plaintiffs claimed damages of **$1,383,673.05** for alleged losses caused or contributed to by the defendant's negligence. [CITE:1]

**What the allegedly negligent maintenance concerned.** The claim arose from a fire that started when a lit cigarette fell from the upper floors of Block 2019, Bukit Batok Street 23 and ignited polystyrene packing material stacked outside the plaintiffs' warehouse, with the fire then spreading into the plaintiffs' premises. [CITE:1] The defendant was engaged by the Housing Development Board to service and maintain the block's fire protection and mechanical ventilation systems, and maintaining the fire hose reel system at the plaintiffs' premises was part of that job. [CITE:1]

The thrust of the claim was that the defendant breached its duty of care to the plaintiffs, as users of the fire hose reel it serviced and maintained, by **failing to ensure that there was any water, or sufficient water, in the fire hose reel nearest to the plaintiffs' premises**, thereby preventing them from using the hose to stop the fire and salvage their property. [CITE:1][CITE:2] The plaintiffs also alleged that the defendant **failed to notice that the non-return valve had been installed in the reverse position**, which would have affected the flow of water in the fire hose. [CITE:2]

Under the defendant's contract with HDB, its duties included conducting regular maintenance and servicing of the fire hose reels in the block to ensure each reel was in good condition and all couplings were watertight, and reporting its findings to HDB, including any finding of lack of water pressure or damaged components in the fire protection system. [CITE:2] Its employees physically tested the relevant fire hose reel on 17 September 2009 and recorded that the components were neither faulty nor jammed and that water pressure was not low, with the only damage noted being the cabinet containing the reel. [CITE:2]

**Outcome for context.** The court held that the defendant had not breached its duty of care, noting that servicing the non-return check valve fell outside the contractual duty and that even if the valve had been inserted wrongly it did not definitively mean no water could flow, because water can flow in both directions if the circular disc in the valve is disengaged. [CITE:9] The claim also failed on causation, because the fire had already spread out of control and one or two working fire hose reels would have been insufficient to contain it, so any breach did not cause or contribute to the plaintiffs' loss. [CITE:3]

As at 2015-12-31, in *Union Concept Manufacturers Pte Ltd and another v Rhythme Technology Pte Ltd* [2015] SGHC 121, the defendant, Rhythme Technology Pte Ltd, relied on its contractual relationship with the Housing Development Board (HDB) — rather than any contract with the plaintiffs — to argue that it did not owe the plaintiffs a duty of care. [CITE:1]

Under that HDB contract, Rhythme was engaged to service and maintain the block's fire protection and mechanical ventilation systems, and maintaining the fire hose reel system at the plaintiffs' premises was part of the job. [CITE:2] Its contractual duties included conducting regular maintenance and servicing so that the fire hose reels were in good condition with watertight couplings, and reporting its findings (including possible low water pressure or damaged components) to HDB. [CITE:1] The HDB contract to service the hose reels outside the plaintiffs' premises did not extend to servicing the non-return check valve. [CITE:3]

The General Division nevertheless held that the defendant did owe a duty of care to the plaintiffs as users of the fire hose reel it serviced and maintained, and dismissed the claim on the grounds that no breach of duty was established and that, in any event, any breach did not cause or contribute to the plaintiffs' loss. [CITE:1] [CITE:7]

As at 2014-12-31, the High Court judge treated Hydro Aquatic as not being an independent contractor because he found that NUS had retained a very high degree of control over the manner in which Hydro Aquatic carried out its work, including its pool-safety obligations. [CITE:12]

The judge applied the control test and examined the contractual tender provisions. These required Hydro Aquatic to perform in accordance with the tender specifications and to the Facility Officer’s satisfaction, required its lifeguards to attend twice-weekly briefings, and allowed the Facility Officer to request additional lifeguards. The judge concluded from this arrangement that NUS had not fully delegated all aspects of pool safety to Hydro Aquatic. [CITE:3]

He also reasoned that the contract had commenced only about two months before the drowning, that Hydro Aquatic was still complying with the requirements imposed on it, and that there was little evidence showing how extensively NUS had supervised Hydro Aquatic’s safety arrangements during that period. [CITE:12]

The Court of Appeal later held that this approach was mistaken: the relevant inquiry was whether NUS controlled the lifeguards themselves, rather than whether NUS controlled Hydro Aquatic, and the contractual provisions did not show that control had passed to NUS. The Court therefore held that Hydro Aquatic was an independent contractor and that the lifeguards remained under its control. [CITE:14] [CITE:19] [CITE:32]

**As at 2026-11-06, the two typical defences described in *BNM* [2014] SGCA 49 are:**

1. **Denying negligence:** the defendant denies that the servant or agent was negligent in the first place. [CITE:5]
2. **Asserting independent-contractor status:** the defendant asserts that the servant or agent was an independent contractor, whose negligence the defendant is not responsible for. [CITE:5]

**How this operated in *BNM*:**

- NUS's defence was that it had delegated management and maintenance of the pool to Hydro as an independent contractor. [CITE:5] NUS's position was that, if Hydro was properly appointed as an independent contractor, NUS would not be vicariously liable for Hydro's negligence, if any. [CITE:4]
- The claims against NUS and Hydro proceeded on the footing of negligence by their servants or agents, in particular the alleged failure to ensure the lifeguards were adequately trained in the use of AED and/or Oxyviva; NUS was also separately alleged to have been negligent in appointing Hydro. [CITE:5]
- Because the negligence found by the judge was that of the lifeguards rather than Hydro, the Court of Appeal said it was no longer strictly relevant or necessary to decide whether Hydro, as distinct from the lifeguards, was an independent contractor vis-à-vis NUS. [CITE:4]
- On review, however, the Court concluded that Hydro was carrying on a business on its own account and was therefore an independent contractor, and that NUS would not have been liable even if causation had been established. [CITE:9]

**For context from later authority:** in *NG HUAT SENG* [2017] SGCA 58, the Court of Appeal confirmed that the orthodox approach requires first a special relationship between defendant and tortfeasor, and the fact that a tortfeasor is an independent contractor will generally, in itself, exclude vicarious liability; only if that first hurdle is passed does the second inquiry — whether the relationship created or significantly enhanced the risk of the tort — arise. [CITE:12][CITE:13]

As at 2026-11-06, in *Hotel Royal @ Queens Pte Ltd trading as Hotel Royal @ Queens v J M Pang & Seah (Pte) Ltd* [2014] SGHC 109 (General Division of the High Court, decided 2 June 2014), the defendant's argument was directed at the scope of its bimonthly inspection duty in the plaintiff's High Tension Switch Gear Room ("HTSGR"). [CITE:2]

**The defendant's own reasoning**

The defendant accepted that it had duties of care in contract and in tort to provide reasonable consultancy services, but disputed both whether it had breached them and the scope of its inspection duty. [CITE:13] Its specific submission was that it was not required to measure humidity levels within the HTSGR. [CITE:4] It pointed out that its bimonthly inspections were carried out under the standard checklist issued by the Energy Market Authority ("EMA") for the EI(R1) Report by Licensed Electrical Worker for Condominiums and Multi-Tenanted Buildings, and that this checklist contained no specific requirement for a Licensed Electrical Worker ("LEW") to check humidity levels in an electrical installation. [CITE:4] On that basis, the defendant contended that, because it was not required to check humidity levels, it was not in breach of its duty for failing to take notice of, and notify the plaintiff of, the evidence of high moisture levels within the HTSGR recorded in the Matcor failure assessment report. [CITE:4] The defendant also argued that the humidity levels inside and outside the HTSGR were the same, which it advanced as a reason why checking for moisture was unnecessary. [CITE:3]

**Why that reasoning did not succeed**

The court distinguished humidity from moisture: humidity refers to the amount of water vapour in the air, whereas moisture means the presence of water in the environment in either gaseous or liquid form. [CITE:4] Equal humidity levels inside and outside the HTSGR therefore did not disprove the existence of high moisture levels there, nor did they avoid the defendant's obligation to take note of the danger signs and alert the plaintiff. [CITE:3] Although the defendant was not required to measure humidity, it could not ignore visible evidence of high moisture such as corrosion, paint blistering, moulds and watermarks, which a professional electrical engineer should have noticed and reported during the bimonthly inspections. [CITE:8] The court also held that the EMA checklist's item 3.6, headed "Danger signs", was an overarching, catch-all provision rather than a limitation on an LEW's duty to detect hazards. [CITE:8] The purpose of the contractual bimonthly inspection was precisely to allow the LEW to detect potential safety risks within the HTSGR and notify the plaintiff so that the plaintiff could act accordingly. [CITE:5] The defendant accordingly breached its duty of care by failing to identify the obvious visual signs of high moisture levels and alert the plaintiff to the associated safety hazards. [CITE:3] [CITE:6]

As at 2026-11-06, the causation defence advanced in *Hotel Royal @ Queens Pte Ltd trading as Hotel Royal @ Queens v J M Pang & Seah (Pte) Ltd* [2014] SGHC 109 was **"novus actus interveniens"** — that is, that the chain of legal causation had been broken so that the flashover losses were not attributable to the Defendant's negligence [CITE:3][CITE:13].

**The defence as argued.** The Defendant submitted that the Plaintiff's repeated refusal to approve and permit a shutdown maintenance inspection ("SM", being maintenance work that could only be carried out with the electricity supply cut off) amounted to unreasonable conduct which constituted a *novus actus interveniens*, breaking the chain of causation and absolving the Defendant of liability for the losses arising from the flashover incident [CITE:3][CITE:10][CITE:13].

**The alternative submission.** In the alternative, the Defendant argued that its repeated failures to conduct a SM were signs of negligence on the Plaintiff's part, so that its liability should be reduced on account of the Plaintiff's contributory negligence [CITE:13].

**The court's treatment of the defence.** The court applied the principle quoted from Lord Reid in *McKew v Holland & Hannens & Cubitts (Scotland) Ltd* [1969] 3 All ER 1621 at 1623, that where the injured person acts unreasonably, his unreasonable conduct may be a *novus actus interveniens* [CITE:6]. It rejected the argument on the facts, holding that the Plaintiff's refusal was not a wholly independent cause of the flashover because the Defendant's own negligence had contributed to that refusal: the Defendant's letters from 2005 and 2006 onwards encouraged the belief that partial discharge measurement ("PDM") testing could replace an SM for certification and licence renewal, and the Defendant's continued certification of fitness without an SM concretised that belief [CITE:6]. The court further found that the Defendant's negligence was the "primary and dominant cause" of the flashover [CITE:11]. Causation was nevertheless established because it was not disputed that conduct of an SM would have averted the flashover incident [CITE:3].

**Outcome.** The defence was therefore not successful as a complete answer to liability, but the court found the Plaintiff contributorily negligent in disregarding the Defendant's repeated recommendations, and apportioned the loss 70% to the Defendant and 30% to the Plaintiff [CITE:5][CITE:8].

As at 2026-11-06, in *BNM (administratrix of the estate of B, deceased) v National University of Singapore and another* [2014] SGHC 5, the General Division of the High Court held that the defendants owed the deceased, who was a lawful entrant (an invitee) at the NUS swimming pool, a duty of care to take reasonable care for his safety [CITE:3][CITE:6]. The claim was treated as one solely under the tort of negligence, occupier's liability having been subsumed within negligence [CITE:19][CITE:14][CITE:15]. The court cautioned that the extent of the duty depends on the facts and circumstances of each case, so its decision should not be taken out of context [CITE:3].

**What the duty required**

- **Warning of unusual dangers:** the duty was to warn lawful entrants of unusual dangers, of which there were none on the facts of this case [CITE:6].
- **Qualified lifeguards:** the duty was to provide qualified lifeguards of reasonable competence according to the standards prevailing at the material time [CITE:6]. On the facts of this particular case, the court held that the duty included providing two properly trained and qualified lifeguards on duty whenever the pool was open for use, and that it was not unreasonable for one of the lifeguards to check entrants' eligibility to use the pool from time to time or to collect fees [CITE:9].
- **Express limit:** the duty did not extend to requiring lifeguards to be trained in the use of the Oxyviva machine and the automated external defibrillator (AED) [CITE:6].

**How the court reasoned about the scope of the duty**

- The court noted that there was no legislation requiring or regulating the provision of lifeguards or safety equipment in swimming pools in June 2007 or as at its 2014 decision, so the issue had to be reasoned from first principles [CITE:3].
- On policy, swimming involves risks and calls for precautions but is not an "extra hazardous activity", and this had to be balanced against the fact that reasonable precautions can be taken without undue or onerous expense [CITE:9].
- In a comparable English case, the court had not considered it necessary that pool attendants watch the pool at all times, nor unreasonable for them to combine supervision duties with collecting tickets and opening cubicle doors [CITE:10].

**Relationship to the general occupier framework**

The Court of Appeal's approach, which the High Court applied here, is that most occupiers who have control over the property and/or the activities carried out there owe lawful entrants a prima facie duty to take reasonable care, with the degree of control being the key qualification, and occupiers are not insurers of the safety of their property [CITE:11][CITE:18]. This is consistent with the way the duty was framed in [2014] SGHC 5 [CITE:3].

**A note on delegation**

NUS's position was that the duty could be delegated, and that it had delegated the supply of lifeguards to Hydro Aquatic under a written contract; NUS also contended that both it and Hydro Aquatic were occupiers of the pool because each had a sufficient degree of control over it [CITE:6][CITE:1]. The supplied passages record that contention, but do not set out the court's conclusion on the delegation and co-occupier questions, nor the outcome of Hydro Aquatic's insurance claim [CITE:6][CITE:13].

As at 2026-11-06, the supplied authority is the General Division of the High Court’s decision of 9 January 2014 in *BNM (administratrix of the estate of B, deceased) v National University of Singapore*, which concerned a drowning at an NUS swimming pool in June 2007; the judge noted that his observations about rescue equipment might not be the same today [CITE:1] [CITE:4].

**1. The basic duty**

Pool operators have a duty to take reasonable care and responsibility for the safety of all who use their pools [CITE:3]. The scope of that duty is not identical for every kind of pool, and both legal proximity and the scope of the duty depend on all the facts and circumstances [CITE:3] [CITE:5]. Owners or operators of large or Olympic-sized pools that are in effect open for public use should provide an adequate system of safety for their users [CITE:5]. A restricted or private pool is not automatically exempt: in this case NUS’s pool, although open only to members and guests, had thousands of potential users, so NUS was treated like a large public pool and, having invited use of the facility, was duty-bound to take steps against its obvious risks [CITE:7].

**2. Lifeguards as the core of the safety system**

An adequate system of safety would normally include properly trained lifeguards stationed at appropriate locations around the pool [CITE:7]. The lifeguards are expected to survey the pool regularly, remain alert and trained to spot swimmers in difficulty, drowning or near-drowning, and intervene promptly with proper techniques [CITE:7]. They should also notice and stop over-exuberant behaviour or horseplay among children or young adults that may endanger swimmers [CITE:7]. Because lifeguards are the first responders to a pool emergency, they should also be trained in basic resuscitation techniques [CITE:7].

Correct positioning matters: the court held that stationing one lifeguard at or along Lane 9, at the opposite length of the pool from the lifeguard near the entrance turnstile, was a reasonable measure, because it allowed observation from different vantage points and placed a lifeguard closer to possible casualties on that side [CITE:15]. The court also held that the two lifeguards should not have been seated together, because that encourages distracting chit-chat [CITE:15]. There was some truth in the submission that the defendants had breached their duty by not ensuring, as an internal NUS post-incident review recommended, that lifeguards were deployed on both sides of the pool and that the equipment was placed beside them [CITE:13].

**3. What “reasonable” means in practice**

The duty included providing two properly trained and qualified lifeguards on duty whenever the pool was open, and it was not unreasonable for one lifeguard to check entrants’ eligibility to use the pool from time to time or to collect fees [CITE:17]. Reasonable precautions must be capable of being taken without undue or onerous expense [CITE:17]. It was also fair, just and reasonable to impose liability on an operator who negligently failed to implement reasonable safety measures, with cost and practicality of implementation being relevant [CITE:7]. Tort liability does not follow automatically from a death at a pool: it arises where the operator has not provided a reasonable system of pool safety [CITE:14].

**4. Different settings, different duties**

Not all pool owners must provide properly qualified lifeguards, because a universal rule would impose an unduly onerous and disproportionate burden [CITE:5]. Particular features, such as children having ready access and frequently using the pool, can change the analysis, and a duty of supervision by parents or adults who can swim may arise in private condominium pools [CITE:5]. A duty of care may also be imposed on those carrying on an organised activity in a pool, such as schoolchildren given swimming lessons as part of an extracurricular programme [CITE:5].

**5. Rescue equipment and higher internal standards**

In June 2007, the reasonably expected standard of care did not extend to providing an automated external defibrillator (AED) and an oxygen resuscitator (Oxyviva machine), together with lifeguards trained in their use, because this was not common or industry practice even for the Singapore Sports Council’s public pools [CITE:4]. There is a public-policy reason not to penalise a defendant that conforms to the industry or acceptable standard of the time merely because it sought to achieve a higher safety standard and failed to reach that higher standard [CITE:14]. On this reasoning, the judge rejected the argument that NUS’s tender specifications, which required the equipment and the training, automatically set a higher tort standard: those requirements created obligations in the first instance between NUS and Hydro Aquatic as contracting parties, and the extent of one person’s obligations to another is inferred from the circumstances of the particular case [CITE:6].

**6. Outsourcing does not end the operator’s responsibility**

The duty to provide properly trained lifeguards was delegable, but NUS would still have been liable if it had been negligent in appointing Hydro Aquatic as the contractor to discharge that duty; the court considered the tender duties to have been comprehensively set out and not open to fault [CITE:16]. NUS nevertheless retained considerable control over how Hydro Aquatic carried out its work, and the “Facility Officer” who could give instructions was an NUS employee exercising supervisory control [CITE:8]. The contract clauses showed a hierarchy of control, a requirement that lifeguards follow NUS staff instructions, and liquidated damages for failures such as not following NUS staff instructions or not remaining alert while on duty, so NUS had contracted for and retained very considerable control rather than delegating the job to an independent contractor [CITE:19]. The court accordingly found that Hydro Aquatic was not an independent contractor and that NUS, having retained a high degree of control, had a duty to continue supervising it, although the contract had been running for only about two months and there was little evidence of the extent of NUS’s supervision of the safety arrangements [CITE:12].

**How the duty was applied**

In applying these duties, the court found the lifeguards clearly negligent for failing to notice that the deceased had stopped swimming and sunk to the bottom, and for remaining unaware of the emergency until a fellow swimmer shouted for help [CITE:15]. The court also found that a further two or three minutes elapsed between the lifeguards reaching the poolside and cardiopulmonary resuscitation beginning, in addition to the time the deceased had spent struggling in the water [CITE:18].

In short, the judgment states that pool operators must maintain a reasonable system of safety matched to the pool and its users, ordinarily involving properly trained lifeguards properly stationed, watchful, and able to intervene and resuscitate; internal standards higher than industry practice do not automatically become the tort standard; and an operator that retains control over how safety services are delivered must continue to supervise its contractor [CITE:3] [CITE:6] [CITE:7] [CITE:12].

As at 2026-11-06, the falling-container judgment is *Tesa Tape Asia Pacific Pte Ltd v Wing Seng Logistics Pte Ltd* [2006] SGHC 73, and the "escape-of-dangerous-things" principle it discusses is the rule in *Rylands v Fletcher*. [CITE:1] [CITE:14]

**The short answer**

Liability attaches to an occupier because the occupier is the person who, for their own purposes, brought onto their land and kept there something likely to do mischief if it escapes; the law therefore requires that occupier to keep it in at their peril and makes them prima facie answerable for all damage that is the natural consequence of its escape. [CITE:3]

**Why this is a liability of the occupier rather than of fault**

The rule is one of strict liability, meaning liability without proof of negligence or other fault. [CITE:1] In *Tesa Tape* the court stated the fundamental proposition in these terms: liability attaches because the occupier of land brings onto the land something which is likely to cause damage if it escapes. [CITE:14] [CITE:20] The court said expressly that fault of the occupier was not an issue when this rule applied, and that fault mattered only for the plaintiff's alternative claim in negligence. [CITE:14] This distinguishes the rule from negligence, where the plaintiff must first establish a duty of care before breach is considered. [CITE:14] Nuisance and the *Rylands v Fletcher* rule are likewise described as not being "fault-based" liabilities, whereas negligence is. [CITE:1] Taking all reasonable care is not by itself a defence to nuisance. [CITE:16]

The underlying rationale is the allocation of risk between landowners. In *Lim Seng Chye v Pex International Pte Ltd* [2019] SGHC 28 the Court of Appeal described the rule as "an aspect of the law of private nuisance" that "derives from the use of land and covers the division of risk as between the owners of the land in question and other landowners", and noted that the essence of property-based torts such as nuisance is risk management in the use of one's property. [CITE:20] [CITE:18] Singapore's High Court has therefore continued to apply the rule as part of the tort of nuisance rather than absorbing it into negligence as the High Court of Australia did in *Burnie*. [CITE:9] [CITE:20]

**The conditions the occupier must satisfy in the container case**

- The occupier must have brought onto the land a thing likely to cause damage if it escapes: in *Tesa Tape*, stacking containers seven tiers high was held to be "a non-natural use of the land, industrial or otherwise". [CITE:3] [CITE:20]
- There must be an escape: in the tort sense, escape means a situation in which things on one's land find themselves in the neighbouring land, and the process by which they move or are moved from one property to the other constitutes escape; the collapse of the containers into the plaintiff's yard was therefore an escape. [CITE:1]
- The damage must be the natural consequence of the escape and must be foreseeable: damage and injury were foreseeable should the containers fall onto the neighbouring land, so the collapse attracted the application of the rule. [CITE:3] [CITE:14] Foreseeability of damage of the relevant type is a prerequisite of liability in damages under the rule. [CITE:11]
- The thing brought on the land must be dangerous: the court considered, drawing on *Hale v Jennings Brothers*, whether the thing was "dangerous in itself", and the later Singapore formulation describes the "thing" as needing to pose an "exceptionally high risk" to neighbouring property should it escape. [CITE:1] [CITE:9]

**One further point on delegation**

An occupier cannot escape liability under nuisance, including within the parameters of the rule, simply by having the work done by an independent contractor, because the blanket exclusion of independent contractors that applies in negligence does not operate in private nuisance. [CITE:11]

**1. The existing approach as the appeal described it**

Singapore, unlike England, allowed recovery of pure economic loss, but the courts advocated a more restricted approach to its recovery, purporting to apply a different test — the “two-stage process” in *Ocean Front* — for such claims, while the three-part *Caparo* test (foreseeability, proximity, fairness) was applied to cases of physical damage. [CITE:2][CITE:4][CITE:19]

The Court of Appeal recorded that, in determining whether to impose a duty of care for pure economic loss, the courts had “consistently adopted a more restrictive approach” and applied the *Ocean Front* two-stage process. [CITE:4]

The reasons given were that pure economic loss is not constrained by the laws of nature and can ripple out through a complex web of human-created economic relationships, creating the concern of “indeterminate liability” — liability in an indeterminate amount, for an indeterminate time, to an indeterminate class — that participants in those relationships can use contracts to allocate risk and the degree of protection they need, and that pure economic loss frequently results in mere transfers of wealth rather than a new loss to social wealth. [CITE:1][CITE:5][CITE:15]

The earlier decision in *United Project Consultants* described the local position as comparatively settled, in contrast to the English courts’ difficulty in choosing between the three-fold test, the incremental approach and assumption of responsibility; the Singapore two-stage structure was: first, whether there is a sufficient degree of proximity giving rise to a duty to avoid the kind of loss sustained; second, whether any material factor or policy precludes that duty. [CITE:7][CITE:9]

**2. The approach the appeal settled on**

A single test now applies whether the loss is pure economic loss or physical damage: stage one, proximity; stage two, policy considerations, to be approached with reference to the facts of decided cases, although the absence of such a case is not an absolute bar to finding a duty. [CITE:20]

Factual foreseeability remains a threshold issue, but the appeal did not include it in the legal test for a duty of care. [CITE:20]

The *Ocean Front* two-stage process was not a reversion to the approach in *Anns*: proximity was not established by foreseeability alone but by consideration of other relevant facts, and the restrictive approach is not triggered merely by the type of damage, because each case must be examined on its own facts. [CITE:4][CITE:6][CITE:10]

**3. Subsequent confirmation**

In *NTUC Foodfare* (2018), the Court of Appeal held that the *Spandeck* test remains the single test for all negligence claims, including relational economic loss, because the proximity requirement already addresses the concern of indeterminate liability and there is therefore no necessity for special criteria beyond proximity. [CITE:12][CITE:15]

In *Ngiam Kong Seng* (2008), the Court of Appeal explained that the second stage asks whether, in the specific context of a case, public policy factors would prevent a duty even where proximity is sufficient; if none applies, the duty is established, subject to the usual constraints on recovery, including remoteness of damage, mitigation and contributory negligence. [CITE:8]

In practice, the courts have generally recognised a duty of care in pure economic loss cases only where the defendant voluntarily assumed responsibility to the plaintiff and/or the plaintiff reasonably relied on the defendant to take care to avoid causing that loss. [CITE:18] The High Court has also noted the English position that courts should be slow to intervene in commercial transactions between parties of equal bargaining power, leaving parties to allocate risks and responsibilities by contract, and the Singapore view that a duty of care for pure economic loss should not be imposed where the situation is entirely contractual in nature. [CITE:13][CITE:16]

Vicarious liability is “derivative liability”: it makes a party legally responsible for another person’s tort without the party itself having committed the specific fault. [CITE:3] It requires an appropriate sufficiently close relationship, and an independent-contractor relationship generally excludes it; merely showing that the employer’s undertaking caused the harm is insufficient. [CITE:11][CITE:18]

However, the employer is not necessarily immune from liability on separate grounds: [CITE:9]

- **Negligent selection** is primary liability for the employer’s own failure to use reasonable care and skill in choosing a suitable contractor, rather than liability for the contractor’s negligence. [CITE:3][CITE:19]
- A **non-delegable duty** is a personal duty that the employer cannot escape merely by delegating the work, although the doctrine does not itself impose a higher or absolute standard of care. [CITE:12]

Thus, the fire judgment establishes that independent-contractor negligence does not automatically create vicarious liability, while leaving open separate liability for negligent selection or breach of a non-delegable duty. [CITE:9][CITE:12]
