**Rent for subdivisions**

- Under section 3(1), every lessee or grantee of land under a State lease or grant must, within one month after obtaining subdivision permission, notify the Collector in writing, provide the approved subdivision plan, and identify the persons beneficially entitled to the subdivided parts. [CITE:1]

- Section 18(1) provides that where two or more persons are joint owners of a material interest in land, each is jointly and severally liable for any land betterment charge concerning that material interest. [CITE:2]

## Architects' Board — Architects Act 1991, s 4E

- A member's office becomes vacant if the member dies, resigns or is removed from office, or becomes disqualified for office within the meaning of section 4D [CITE:1].
- **Filling the vacancy:** where a vacancy arises among the elected or appointed members, the **Minister must, as soon as practicable, appoint any registered architect** to fill it [CITE:1].
- **Term of the vacancy appointee:** the person appointed holds office only for **the remainder of the term for which the predecessor was elected or appointed** [CITE:1].
- The Board may, with the Minister's approval, remove a member who is absent without leave from three consecutive ordinary meetings of the Board or of a Disciplinary Committee of which the member is a member [CITE:1].
- Any question as to whether a person has ceased to be a Board member is decided by the **Minister**, whose decision is final [CITE:1].
- A vacancy does not affect the Board's powers, and no act done under the Board's authority is invalid merely because a defect in the appointment, election or qualification of members is later discovered [CITE:1].

## Land Surveyors Board — Land Surveyors Act 1991, s 4

- All members of the Land Surveyors Board are **appointed by the Minister**, including a president drawn from among the registered surveyors, three registered surveyors selected from a list submitted by the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers, and not more than three other registered surveyors as the Minister determines [CITE:2].
- **Appointment term:** a member of the Board is appointed **for a term not exceeding 2 years**, may be re-appointed, and may at any time be removed from office by the Minister [CITE:2].
- **Filling a vacancy:** any vacancy must, as soon as practicable, be filled **in the manner in which the appointment to the vacant office was made**, and the person so appointed holds office for **the remainder of the term for which the predecessor was appointed** [CITE:2].
- Any question as to whether a person has ceased to be a member is decided by **the Board itself**, whose decision is final [CITE:2].
- A vacancy does not affect the Board's powers [CITE:2].

## 1. Survey records may be maintained electronically

Section 6(3) of the Boundaries and Survey Maps Act 1998 ("BSMA") provides that the survey records and plans for any land may be maintained by the Chief Surveyor in any electronic media or other means [CITE:1]. Section 6(1)(b) also imposes the duty to maintain all survey records, and section 6(1)(c) requires copies of survey records and plans to be made available on payment of the prescribed fees [CITE:1]. The Act therefore leaves the storage medium open, permitting electronic records rather than mandating paper.

## 2. A caveat affecting part of a survey lot needs an annexed plan

Section 8(3) of the Registration of Deeds Act 1988 ("RDA") requires that, where a part of a Government survey lot is affected, the caveat must have a plan annexed edging with sufficient identity that part of the lot affected [CITE:2]. Section 8(4)(b) adds that the Registrar must not register a caveat which fails to state the Government survey lot number maintained in the Chief Surveyor's records, or, where part of a lot is affected, fails to state that part of the existing lot and fails to clearly identify that part in one or more plans annexed to the caveat [CITE:2]. The lot number referred to is the lot number assigned by the Chief Surveyor under section 6(1)(a) of the BSMA [CITE:1]. Section 6 governs the Chief Surveyor's internal record-keeping duties and expressly permits records and plans to be kept electronically or by other means [CITE:1]. Section 8 governs the substantive conditions that a caveat must satisfy before the Registrar will register it, and for a part-lot caveat those conditions include an annexed plan that both edges the affected part with sufficient identity and clearly identifies it [CITE:2]. ### Carbon Pricing Act: reportable-facility deregistration

A registered person may apply to the Agency to deregister a business facility as a **reportable facility** where the facility’s total reckonable greenhouse-gas emissions have a carbon dioxide equivalent that **does not attain the first emissions threshold in each of three consecutive years**. As at 2026-11-06, section 37 of the Carbon Pricing Act 2018 and section 6 of the Fisheries Act 1966 provide for different appellate forums, different limits on the grounds of appeal, and different degrees of finality [CITE:1][CITE:2].

## Carbon Pricing Act 2018 — appeal to the General Division of the High Court

**Who hears the appeal.** A registered person aggrieved by certain decisions of the Agency may first appeal to the Minister, who may establish an Appeal Panel where the appeal involves technical or specialised issues [CITE:5]. The Minister or the Appeal Panel may confirm, vary or reverse the Agency's decision, or direct the Agency to reconsider it [CITE:3]. Section 37 then permits the appellant (the registered person) **or the Agency** to appeal to the **General Division of the High Court** from a decision of the Minister or an Appeal Panel [CITE:1].

**Permitted basis.** The appeal may be brought "upon any question of law or of mixed law and fact", so the permitted basis is confined to legal questions or questions combining law and fact, and the section does not provide for an appeal on purely factual grounds [CITE:1]. There is also a monetary threshold: section 37(1) does not apply where the Ministerial or Appeal Panel decision results in a change of less than 250 tCO2e × R in the amount of tax charged, where R is the carbon tax rate used for the emissions year in question [CITE:1]. The Act defines "carbon dioxide equivalence", in relation to any greenhouse gas, as the mass of the greenhouse gas multiplied by its global warming potential set out in the First Schedule [CITE:8].

**Finality.** The determination of the Minister or Appeal Panel is final **unless section 37 applies** [CITE:3]. Where section 37 does apply, the General Division must hear and determine the appeal and may confirm, vary or annul the decision, and make any further or other order as to costs or otherwise that it considers fit [CITE:1]. Procedure and costs are governed by the Rules of Court [CITE:1], and there is a further right of appeal from the General Division on the same basis as exists for decisions the General Division makes in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction [CITE:1].

## Fisheries Act 1966 — appeal to the Minister

**Who hears the appeal.** The Director-General may issue licences, refuse to issue a licence, vary or impose additional conditions, or revoke a licence already issued [CITE:2]. Any person aggrieved by such a refusal, variation or revocation may appeal to the **Minister, whose decision "shall be final"** [CITE:2].

**Permitted basis.** Section 6(3) states no restriction on the grounds of the appeal: it identifies only that the appellant must be "aggrieved" by the refusal, variation or revocation, with no equivalent to the law-only or law-and-fact limitation, and no monetary threshold equivalent to the 250 tCO2e × R threshold in section 37 [CITE:2][CITE:1].

**Finality.** The Minister's decision is final, and section 6(4) provides that no action or proceeding shall be maintainable in any court of law in respect of such a refusal, variation or revocation [CITE:2]. Section 6 therefore provides no route of appeal from the Minister's decision to the General Division, in contrast with section 37 of the Carbon Pricing Act [CITE:2][CITE:1].

## Summary of the differences

- **Forum:** the General Division of the High Court hears a Carbon Pricing Act appeal from the Minister or Appeal Panel [CITE:1], whereas the Minister hears a Fisheries Act appeal and no further appeal is provided for under that section [CITE:2].
- **Grounds:** Carbon Pricing Act appeals are limited to questions of law or mixed law and fact, and are unavailable below a stated monetary change in tax charged [CITE:1]; the Fisheries Act appeal is confined only to the categories of licensing decision and the requirement of being aggrieved [CITE:2].
- **Who may appeal:** the Agency as well as the appellant may bring the section 37 appeal [CITE:1], while only an aggrieved person may appeal to the Minister under section 6 [CITE:2].
- **Finality:** the Carbon Pricing route is final at the Ministerial or Appeal Panel stage only where section 37 does not apply, and a further appeal lies from the General Division where section 37 does apply [CITE:3][CITE:1]; the Fisheries route ends with the Minister's final decision, coupled with a bar on court proceedings [CITE:2].

### What the appellate court decided on liability for the first flood

- The appeal concerned the General Division’s dismissal of SRA’s counterclaim for the first flood; the Court of Appeal affirmed the main holding that SSA was not liable to SRA for the alleged losses arising from that flood [CITE:1] [CITE:11].

- The General Division had found that SSA had breached its duty to take reasonable care to maintain the condition and safety of the Premises after the renovation works, but that the breach had not caused the first flood [CITE:1] [CITE:16].

- The Court of Appeal’s own discussion accepted that, from 1 December 2014 when SSA regained control, SSA had a duty to monitor and supervise the condition of the Premises, to make reasonable inquiries about the scope and soundness of the renovation works, and to check that they had been completed to a satisfactory standard; it recorded that there was no evidence SSA had made any such inquiry or check [CITE:3].

- Its decisive reasoning was that control by SSA over the Premises during the renovation period had not been proved, and that neither causal proximity nor any voluntary assumption of responsibility by SSA with concomitant reliance by SRA had been established [CITE:17].

- The Court of Appeal added that the main cause of the first flood was the landslip at the embankment between Culverts B and C, triggered by poor design and/or poor construction; Sport SG had engaged HCJ to carry out the works, SSA was not involved in designing or constructing the drain or embankment and had no control or oversight, and after regaining control SSA neither knew nor could reasonably have been expected to know of the defects [CITE:14].

- It also held, as an independent ground, that SSA could not be said to have caused the alleged losses suffered by SRA from the first flood [CITE:11].

- SRA’s contention that indiscriminate dumping of earth fill and debris caused the first flood was irrelevant, because the judge’s finding that the dumping was not causative had not been challenged on appeal and the evidence did not conclusively establish that SSA was responsible for any dumping [CITE:11].

- In short, both courts reached the same outcome of no liability for SSA on the first flood, although the appellate judgment rested additionally on the absence of proved control during the renovation period and the absence of causal proximity and reliance, rather than only on the General Division’s breach-and-“but for” causation analysis [CITE:15] [CITE:16] [CITE:17].

- As to costs, the Court of Appeal found no good reason to disturb the order that SRA pay SSA the costs of the proceedings below fixed at $85,600 plus reasonable disbursements, and ordered SRA to pay SSA the costs of the appeal fixed at $30,000 inclusive of disbursements [CITE:11] [CITE:20].

- The appeal did not concern the General Division’s award of $4,708 to SRA for cleaning works after the second flood of 3 May 2015, which rested on the SSA’s failure to maintain the drain and to undertake adequate rectification or precautionary measures after the first flood [CITE:1] [CITE:10] [CITE:12].

### 1. What the entrant must establish under [2018] SGCA 42

Occupiers’ liability is governed by the law of negligence and the two-stage Spandeck framework. [CITE:8] The first stage asks whether sufficient legal proximity exists between the occupier and entrant, taking account of physical, circumstantial and causal proximity, including any voluntary assumption of responsibility and reliance. [CITE:8] An occupier’s control over the premises is relevant but not necessarily determinative, and the ultimate question is whether the particular occupier ought to owe the particular entrant a prima facie duty of care. [CITE:9] [CITE:12] [CITE:13]

For a lawful entrant—that is, an entrant whose circumstances of entry can be established as lawful on a balance of probabilities—occupiers with control will usually owe a prima facie duty of care because physical and circumstantial proximity will ordinarily be present. [CITE:5] Where the entrant’s lawfulness cannot be definitively established, the court applies the fact-sensitive Spandeck analysis to determine whether a duty should nevertheless be imposed. [CITE:5]

Beyond establishing a duty, the entrant must establish two further elements: **breach of duty and causation**. [CITE:6]

- **Breach:** The occupier must have failed to exercise reasonable care to eliminate a danger that it actually knew or ought reasonably to have known about; an occupier is not an insurer of the safety of either the property or people entering it. [CITE:13] [CITE:7]
- **Causation:** On a balance of probabilities, the entrant must show that the loss would not have occurred but for the occupier’s negligent acts or omissions. [CITE:6]

Accordingly, the occurrence of harm does not by itself establish occupier liability: the entrant must also prove both a failure to take reasonable care and the required causal connection. [CITE:6] In [2018] SGCA 42, the Court of Appeal held that SSA was not liable in negligence for the first flood. [CITE:6]

### 2. The safety duty stated for pool operators in [2014] SGHC 5

In [2014] SGHC 5, the court held that the pool operators owed a duty to lawful entrants to take reasonable care for their safety. [CITE:16] More generally, pool operators have a duty to take reasonable care and responsibility for the safety of everyone who uses their pools. [CITE:19]

The precise scope depends on the pool and its circumstances; owners and operators of all types of swimming pools are not subject to an identical duty. [CITE:18] [CITE:19] In particular:

- Owners or operators of large or Olympic-sized pools commonly used in public complexes should provide an adequate system of safety for their users. [CITE:18]
- There is no universal rule requiring every pool owner to provide properly qualified lifeguards, because that would impose an unduly onerous burden on some owners in circumstances where it would not be proportionate to the expected benefits. [CITE:18]
- The pool’s type, access, users and their ages and abilities all matter; for example, children with ready access to a pool may raise different considerations from adult users of a private pool. [CITE:18] [CITE:19]
- At the material time, the judge observed that no legislation required or regulated the provision of lifeguards or safety equipment in swimming pools, leaving the court to determine the duty from first principles. [CITE:16]

The standard was one of reasonableness rather than guaranteed safety. On the facts of that case, it was not reasonable to expect the operators to provide an AED and an Oxyviva machine or to provide lifeguards properly trained in their use; the judge also considered that an operator who met the industry standard should not be penalised merely because it sought to exceed that standard but failed to achieve the higher standard. [CITE:20]

In short, [2018] SGCA 42 requires a lawful entrant to prove **duty, breach and causation**, while [2014] SGHC 5 describes pool operators’ duty as taking reasonable care and responsibility for pool safety, including an adequate safety system for large or public pools, with its scope determined by the particular facts. [CITE:6] [CITE:18] [CITE:19]

As at 2026-11-06, the 2022 decision rejected MCST’s reliance on Zoe to excuse its own safety responsibility, while the 2008 decision held that the direct employer had not provided the worker with a safe system of work and therefore could not fault him for the working method it had failed to design [CITE:5] [CITE:16].

**MCST’s independent-contractor defence**

MCST argued that it had not breached its duty of care because it could reasonably rely on Zoe, its independent contractor, to provide a safe system of work, the necessary safety equipment, and supervision [CITE:5].

The Appellate Division rejected that argument: as the occupier, MCST had primary responsibility for safety in the M&E Room and could not avoid liability by “sheltering behind” Zoe [CITE:5]. This reflected the WSH Regime’s more direct allocation of responsibility to those who create or control workplace safety risks [CITE:8].

**Hao Wei’s safe-system-of-work reasoning**

In *Hao Wei*, the High Court held that the employer had not provided the employee with a safe system of work because it had neither given precise instructions on how the metal formworks should be removed manually nor provided additional workers to assist him [CITE:16].

Accordingly, it was not open for the employer to argue that the employee was contributorily negligent for adopting the straddling position rather than the scaffold position, because the employer had not devised a safe system in the first place [CITE:16]. There was also no evidence that the straddling position was more likely to cause injury, and the employee’s conduct was characterised as an error of judgment rather than culpable neglect [CITE:16].

The later *Janaed* decision added an important qualification: an employer’s failure to provide a safe system does not automatically eliminate any possibility of contributory negligence, because that issue remains fact-sensitive and is assessed using common sense [CITE:12]. In *Janaed* itself, the 30% contributory-negligence finding was upheld [CITE:17].

As at 2026-11-06, the two judgments start from different contractual positions but both treat the scope of the duty of care as depending on the defendant's actual obligations and the surrounding circumstances. [CITE:1][CITE:11]

## 1. The fire-hose maintenance judgment: [2015] SGHC 121 [CITE:1][CITE:2]

- **The contractual reason for denying a duty:** Rhythme Technology argued that its contract was with the Housing Development Board (HDB), and that it therefore owed the plaintiffs no duty of care. [CITE:1][CITE:2]
- **The court's answer:** The court rejected that argument as a complete answer, holding that the company did owe the plaintiffs a duty of care as users of the fire hose reel it serviced and maintained; the live question was the extent of that duty. [CITE:1]
- **How the contract defined the extent of the duty:** Under the HDB contract, the defendant's duties included regular maintenance and servicing of the fire hose reels in the block to keep them in good condition with watertight couplings, and reporting findings to HDB, including possible lack of water pressure or damaged components in the fire protection system. [CITE:1]
- **Where that duty stopped:** The HDB contract did not extend to servicing the non-return check valve, and the court treated other explanations for a poor flow of water — such as the hose reel not being properly disentangled or the tap not being properly turned on — as falling outside the defendant's duty of care. [CITE:5]
- **Outcome on these issues:** The court found no breach of the duty of care, and held that the claim would fail on causation in any event because the fire was already out of control and one or two hose reels, even if fully working, would not have contained it. [CITE:5][CITE:6]

## 2. The supervision duty found in [2006] SGHC 222 [CITE:13][CITE:15]

- **The defendant's contractual argument:** The architect/consultant argued that his legal responsibilities were confined to the duties he owed as QP and to his legal relationship with the main contractor, PMC, who was his employer; he also contended that it was highly unusual for a building owner to appoint the architect engaged by the main contractor to supervise that contractor. [CITE:14]
- **Why the court rejected it:** Clause 1 of the Deed stated that "The Consultants warrant that they shall exercise reasonable skill, care and diligence in the performance of their duties to the Contractor and/or the Employer," and the court held that this was not a mere restatement of duties already owed as QP or to PMC; the plaintiff required the Deed precisely because it gave it additional legal protection, and the court sought to give effect to the clause's plain language read in context. [CITE:20][CITE:13]
- **The supervision duty found:** The defendant owed the plaintiff a duty of care to assist in ensuring that the main contractor fulfilled its obligations under the "design and build contract", which included the proper supervision of the main contractor's work and the exercise of reasonable skill, care and diligence. [CITE:15][CITE:13]
- **Which clause carried the duty:** The duty arose under clause 1; clause 4 was a separate and independent indemnity clause presupposing liability incurred by the plaintiff to a third party, and imposed no duty of care. [CITE:10]
- **Breach found:** There were numerous reminders complaining that the defendant had not exercised the requisite degree of supervision, he was aware of the actual situation on site, the main contractor did not perform up to expectations and damage followed; the court also found he failed to fulfil his certification duties, failed to apply for the Temporary Occupation Permit, and failed to issue the requisite Certificate of Supervision within the stipulated statutory period. [CITE:10]
- **Temporal reach of the duty:** The court treated the supervision duty as a continuing one that extended beyond the contractual completion date, and accordingly held the plaintiff's claim was not time-barred. [CITE:9][CITE:11]

## 3. The comparison [CITE:1][CITE:20]

In the fire-hose case, the defendant relied on a contract with HDB rather than with the injured parties, yet the court still found a duty of care in tort, with its content bounded by what the HDB contract actually required of the defendant. [CITE:1][CITE:5] In the Sunny Metal case, the defendant resisted liability by pointing to the limits of his existing professional and employment duties, but the court found that his separate Deed created a duty of care extending to proper supervision of the main contractor's work, and that this contractual undertaking was itself a principal basis for the concurrent tort duty of care. Resource Piling pleaded that the inaccurate information caused it to underprice the piling works and subsequently incur additional rock-socketing costs, construction difficulties and delays. [CITE:1] The judgment formally framed the legal issues as whether Geospecs owed Resource Piling a duty to ensure the logs were accurate and, if so, whether that duty was breached. [CITE:7]

### DSTA: contractual-administration negligence

DSTA was appointed the project’s **superintending officer**, with contractual responsibilities for administering and supervising the project and certifying interim payments for Spandeck’s work. [CITE:3]

Spandeck’s pleaded case was that it **depended on DSTA to value and certify its work accurately**, and that DSTA could not be absolved from liability for negligence in that administrative function. [CITE:4] The supplied passages state this allegation at a general level and do not identify a particular disputed valuation or payment said to have been handled incorrectly. [CITE:3] [CITE:4]

### Central contrast

The Resource Piling case focused on the **accuracy of underlying soil information before tender and the contractor’s foreseeable reliance on it**, with the alleged breach occurring in the investigation and preparation of the logs. [CITE:1] [CITE:17] [CITE:18] The Spandeck case instead focused on DSTA’s **exercise of its administrative and certification functions over work being performed**, rather than on the preparation of soil data. As at 2026-11-06, *BNM* corrected the level at which control must be assessed for vicarious liability, while *Lim Seng Chye* explained the consequence of establishing that a contractor is genuinely independent.[CITE:1][CITE:4][CITE:15]

### *BNM*: the Judge’s control-related reason

The trial Judge adopted the control test and found that NUS had retained a “significant degree of control” over the manner in which Hydro carried out its work. His conclusion was that NUS had not fully delegated all aspects of pool safety to an independent contractor.[CITE:5]

The problem identified by the Court of Appeal was that the Judge examined NUS’s control over **Hydro as a company**, rather than NUS’s control over the **lifeguards whose negligence was alleged**; the tender provisions he considered included requirements concerning work to the Facility Officer’s satisfaction, briefings, and deployment of additional lifeguards.[CITE:5][CITE:11]

The Court of Appeal held that the correct inquiry was whether NUS’s control over the lifeguards displaced the presumption that Hydro, their employer, was vicariously liable for their negligence; the distinction between being able to tell a worker **what to do** and controlling **how the work is done** was significant.[CITE:11][CITE:16][CITE:2]

Applying a broader set of factors—including Hydro’s ownership of its business and personnel, scheduling, supervision, training, equipment, and authority over how the lifeguards worked—the Court of Appeal concluded that Hydro was an independent contractor and that NUS was not vicariously liable.[CITE:7][CITE:13]

### *Lim Seng Chye*: the stated limit on vicarious liability

The fire judgment stated that “[t]he imposition of vicarious liability for the acts of independent contractors can never be justified on the basis of the theory of enterprise risk”. Its reasoning was that an independent contractor operates outside the hirer’s organisation and carries on business on its own account, so the risks arising from the contractor’s conduct should remain with the contractor.[CITE:15]

The court also stated that independent-contractor status will generally, in itself, be sufficient to exclude vicarious liability; the objectives of compensating victims and deterring future harm through vicarious liability are not achieved by making a hirer answer for the acts of genuine independent contractors.[CITE:18]

This was a limit specifically on **vicarious liability**, not a blanket exclusion of direct negligence or non-delegable-duty claims, which the fire judgment considered separately.[CITE:17][CITE:20]

The two propositions are therefore complementary rather than inconsistent: *BNM* explains that control must be assessed over the actual employees and whether their employer’s vicarious-liability presumption has been displaced, while *Lim Seng Chye* states that genuine independent-contractor status generally excludes vicarious liability.[CITE:11][CITE:13][CITE:15][CITE:18]

As at 2026-11-06, the supplied authorities support the position that directorship is not a form of immunity from personal tort liability, although it does not by itself establish liability. [CITE:5][CITE:8][CITE:10]

**Director status and personal liability**

- The 2018 High Court distinguished liability for a director’s **own tort** from liability arising merely from the company’s tort. A director who personally commits a tort may be personally liable, and the company may also be vicariously liable; being a director is irrelevant to that personal liability once the elements of the tort are established. [CITE:6][CITE:8]
- For negligent misrepresentation, however, personal liability requires more than a special relationship with the company or a statement made in the director’s corporate capacity. There must be an indication that the director personally assumed responsibility for the statement. [CITE:5][CITE:7][CITE:10]
- In *Haw Wan Sin*, the High Court found that Jimmy Sim made the relevant representation as Faber’s director, that the appellants treated it as a representation by Faber, and that there was therefore insufficient personal proximity for a duty of care to arise; personal liability was accordingly rejected on those facts. [CITE:1]
- In the later 2019 Court of Appeal appeal, however, the court treated the issue as one of the director’s personal tort and concluded that Jimmy Sim had assumed personal responsibility because he made the representations knowing that the appellants were interested in investing, without disclaiming personal responsibility. Whether a director has assumed personal responsibility is fact-specific. [CITE:16][CITE:20]

**Duties concerning pure economic loss**

- *United Project Consultants* concerned an auditor and tax agent rather than a director, but provided the general framework for negligent claims seeking “pure economic loss”—financial loss rather than injury to person or property—and treated such claims more restrictively than claims involving personal injury or property damage. [CITE:3][CITE:4][CITE:13]
- The Court of Appeal described the English authorities as confused because three different approaches had been used: a threefold test of foreseeability, proximity and fairness; an incremental approach; and an assumption-of-responsibility approach. It considered the inconsistent application of these tests unsatisfactory. [CITE:17]
- The court’s own approach made **proximity** the touchstone: the question was not merely whether a duty existed in general, but whether the circumstances established a relationship requiring the defendant to avoid the particular loss complained of, with no policy reason against imposing that duty. It expressly stated that this was not a return to the two-stage test associated with *Anns v Merton London Borough Council*. [CITE:15]
- In the 2018 director case, proximity was examined through two questions: whether the director had assumed responsibility in a personal capacity or merely for the company, and whether the parties had intended to exclude personal tort liability. Physical proximity was accepted, while circumstantial proximity was doubtful but immaterial because the capacity issue was determinative. [CITE:9]
- The 2018 court also rejected the argument that corporate status required either universal director liability or complete director immunity, and accepted that positive policy considerations could reinforce a finding of duty. [CITE:8][CITE:10]

The two approaches therefore fit together: *United Project Consultants* supplied the general proximity framework for pure economic loss, while *Haw Wan Sin* applied that framework to distinguish a director’s personal responsibility from responsibility attributed only to the company. [CITE:9][CITE:15]
